Not sharing the prompts since it's not my app, but I'll do you one better and share the method behind them. Thank you @SyntexRl for being a good sport!

👉 If you want more examples and actual prompts, see the pinned article on my profile, it's got lots more detail!

Obviously, this is a rough prototype, missing lots of features and personality from the original. Check out @lockedintheapp for the real thing.

--

Prompt 1: Lay out the design system with intentionality

AI lacks taste but that doesn't mean it's bad at design. The problem is when you ask AI to fill in gaps and let it do whatever it wants. If you provide a clear vision, AI can bring it to life.

In this case, I liked what @SyntexRl was doing with pixel art. But the rest of the app didn't match (standard gradients and cards). I wanted to go all-in on the gamified pixel art feel.

If you want your app to be bold and stand out, you have to prompt boldly. With AI, you can take risks, like asking for a custom pixel art UI library. Doing that by hand would take weeks. Claude can knock it out in 10 minutes. If you hate it, just throw it out. Don't be afraid.

I prompted Claude to follow the pixel art aesthetic, with clear instructions about how each screen and component. It was long and detailed, which gave Claude plenty to anchor to when it needed to fill gaps. The one-shot output was already 90% of the way there.

--

Prompt 2: Minor refinements

There will always be things you and the AI weren't aligned on. If you leave it like that, users will spot the rough edges right away. AI puts unnecessary extras in, mixes fonts excessively, wraps things in cards for no reason, etc.

Claude did all of those things and I had to give it specific guidance: make the buttons the same sizes, right-align things in cards, clean up typography.

Fonts are tough for AI to get right. My trick is to have Claude build an HTML page or debug screen with font options in context, pick my favorites, and hone in, rather than describing fonts with words.

Dialing in the pixel dither effects took eyeballing and explanation because it was so foreign to Claude. But I didn't want to settle for normal gradients, so I think it was worth the effort.

--

Prompt 3: The Add Habit card transition

Claude defaulted to a standard slide up/down animation for the bottom sheet. This looked fine but boring, and I saw an opportunity for a unique transition. I described this to Claude as a "pixellated wipe/reveal shader" and it understood what I meant somehow. I also explained that I wanted it to be interactively driven by the user dragging on the card, and that it needed to verify this behavior in the simulator, which was important for it to work through the issues and nail it first try.

--

Prompt 4: Finishing touches

Nothing special, just pointed out a bunch of small things I didn't like before recording (corner radii, button size/alignment, ugly pixel effects)

THIS CHINESE GUY BUILT A SYSTEM WHERE CLAUDE BUILDS, TESTS, AND FIXES ITS OWN CODE IN A LOOP UNTIL IT'S ACTUALLY PERFECT

Most people don't realize their AI coding agent runs once and hands you whatever comes out, bugs included.

He built a system that doesn't stop until the code is actually correct.

Two specialized agents in Claude Code:

→ Builder Agent: only writes and fixes code.
→ Checker Agent: only runs tests, type checks, and linting. Reports exactly what failed.

They're kept separate on purpose. An agent checking its own code can't catch its own blind spots.

An orchestrator command chains them into a loop:

→ Builder implements the feature
→ Checker runs everything
→ All green? Loop stops.
→ Something failed? Sent back to Builder. Fixed. Checked again. Repeat.

The critical detail most people miss: stop rules.

Max 5 cycles. After that, a human steps in.

If a fix breaks something that was previously passing, the loop stops immediately. Without this, agents start weakening tests just to fake a pass instead of actually fixing the bug.

This is what an actual autonomous dev workflow looks like. Not one-shot prompting. A real build-test-fix loop with guardrails.

Bookmark this post. Full setup is in the video below.

How can economists best make use of /goal in Codex and Claude Code?

I made a video demonstrating how I converted Kirill Borusyak's (@borusyak) Stata/Python DiD imputation package with a ~15 hour Codex goal left running overnight.

Now, this is a task you can likely one shot: i.e. /goal convert this package to R, verify everything lines up.

However, I find it helpful to define the validation criteria up front rather than leaving it to the coding agent to decide.

In our case, an existing Stata/Python package are helpful for pinning down the expected behavior of an R  package.

In more complex situations, I also recommend using Codex/Claude Code to help you think of validation criteria which would be helpful for "goal"s and how to acquire those criteria.

In the video, I also demo my preferred way of using Codex and Claude Code together (using Claude Code from within Codex), as well using a skill I've made using ChatGPT Pro to get a review of some intermediate work.

Open-weight models are now cheap enough and capable enough to win most work, even while closed models still win the invisible layer: judgment per prompt.

That is the real point. The draft already has the ingredients, but the current version slightly blurs four separate claims:

GLM‑5.2 is a major open-weight jump. True and supportable.
It still costs more turns than GPT‑5.5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 for some tasks. Strong experiential claim, but needs sharper language.
Benchmarks miss something important. Excellent point. Needs a name.
The Fable 5 shutdown gave https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F a market opening. Very strong, but should be phrased as “helped create” rather than “gave,” unless you want a deliberately provocative take.

https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s own GLM‑5.2 release page on Hugging Face describes it as a substantial leap over GLM‑5.1 for long-horizon tasks, with a 1M-token context window, flexible effort levels, stronger coding, and an MIT open-source license. Its benchmark table also shows big jumps over GLM‑5.1, including Terminal Bench 2.1 rising from 63.5 to 81.0.  Anthropic, meanwhile, launched Fable 5 on June 9, called it its most capable generally available model, then marked Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access unavailable on June 12.  Reuters and The Verge reported that the suspension followed a U.S. government directive limiting access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 over national-security concerns.

1. Core thesis upgrade

Your current thesis:

GLM 5.2 is great, but you need more prompts than with GPT 5.5 or Opus 4.8.

Better thesis:

GLM‑5.2 narrows the capability gap, but not the judgment gap.

Even better:

GLM‑5.2 proves open-weight models can now do most work. GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 still prove that the frontier is not just raw capability — it is judgment density.

Best:

The next model war is not benchmark score. It is prompts-to-done.

That phrase, prompts-to-done, should anchor the post. It captures the whole thing.

Benchmarks ask:

Can the model solve the task?

Real users ask:

How many times do I have to steer it before it becomes usable?

That is the missing layer.

2. Name the thing benchmarks miss

Your line is good:

“Call it taste, instinct, attention to detail.”

Make it sharper by naming the class:

judgment density

Meaning:

How much correct intent, taste, prioritisation, self-correction and finishing instinct the model packs into each turn.

Other strong terms:

TermMeaningPrompt economyHow much useful work you get per prompt.Judgment densityHow much taste, prioritisation and correctness appear in each response.Turn taxThe extra prompting needed to get an open model over the line.Friction gapThe difference between “can do it” and “gets it done cleanly.”Intent compressionHow well the model infers the real task from imperfect instructions.Taste layerThe model’s ability to choose what matters without being told.Finishing instinctWhether it closes loops and polishes the output without nudging.Prompt-to-done ratioNumber of user turns required to reach production-quality output.
Best phrase:
GLM‑5.2 is closing the benchmark gap. The closed labs still lead on prompt economy.
That is very strong.
3. The “three or four prompts vs one prompt” point is the heart
This is your best observation. Make it more explicit:
The difference is not always whether GLM‑5.2 can do the task. Often it can. The difference is that GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 understands the shape of the task sooner. It makes fewer bland choices, catches more missing constraints, preserves taste better, and arrives closer to “done” in one pass.
That is the invisible advantage.
OpenAI’s GPT‑5.5 system card says GPT‑5.5 is designed for complex real-world work and, relative to earlier models, “understands the task earlier,” asks for less guidance, uses tools more effectively, checks its work and keeps going until done.  Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 launch similarly foregrounded judgment: early testers said it asks better questions, catches its own mistakes, pushes back when a plan is unsound, and flags uncertainty more reliably.

That gives you the perfect support for the argument:

The closed labs still win because they reduce the number of steering interventions.

4. Stronger opening

Original:

GLM 5.2 is a massive jump from GLM 5.1.

Better:

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump. But the real story is not the benchmark jump — it is the turn tax.

Or:

GLM‑5.2 is the first open-weight model in a while that made me change my routing. But it still has a hidden cost: prompts.

Or best:

GLM‑5.2 is good enough to change the model market. It is not yet good enough to erase the judgment gap.

That opening has tension.

5. Best rewritten version

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump from GLM‑5.1.But there is a tradeoff people are not talking about: the turn tax.GLM‑5.2 can often accomplish the work. The issue is that you may need three or four prompts to get what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 would often land in one.That gap does not always show up cleanly on benchmarks. Benchmarks measure whether a model can solve a task. Real work measures how much steering it needs before the output becomes https://t.co/DebLt40L8l it taste. Call it instinct. Call it attention to detail. I think the better name is judgment density: the ability to infer what matters, make the right default choices, preserve context, catch edge cases, and finish the job without being hand-held.Closed labs still have more of that.But the shift is real. We are entering an era where cheaper open-weight models can handle most everyday work. Fable 5 was overkill for 80% of vibe-coding tasks anyway. GLM‑5.2 does not need to be the best model in the world to be the model people use all day.And the timing matters. The Fable 5 shutdown created a sudden gap in the market. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F walked straight through it.The lesson should be obvious: when you remove the best closed model from the hands of builders, you do not stop capability diffusion. You accelerate substitution.Restore Fable 5.

6. More aggressive version

GLM‑5.2 is not Fable 5. That is not the point.The point is that it is now close enough for most work and cheap enough to become default infrastructure.Yes, there is still a judgment gap. You can feel it immediately. GLM‑5.2 often needs three or four prompts to do what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 lands in https://t.co/yLcY53IWI3 misses small intent. It needs more steering. It has less taste. It does not always know which detail matters before you tell it.But that is not the same as being unusable. That is the https://t.co/4zj9N4gqan models do not have to beat frontier closed models everywhere. They only have to be good enough, cheap enough, available enough and uncensored enough for builders to route real work through them.Fable 5 was overkill for most vibe coding. GLM‑5.2 is enough for most of it.The U.S. government did not kill demand by forcing Fable 5 offline. It redirected demand.GLM‑5.2 walked into the vacuum.Unban Fable 5.

7. More measured, credible version

GLM‑5.2 is a major open-weight jump, but it also exposes the part of model quality benchmarks still https://t.co/us7jh4dTP5 raw capability, the gap is shrinking fast. GLM‑5.2 can handle a lot of real coding and agentic work that would have been unrealistic for open models not long ago.But in use, there is still a difference between “can solve” and “gets it right in one pass.” GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 often have better prompt economy: they infer intent sooner, preserve taste better, notice missing constraints, and require fewer steering turns.That invisible layer — taste, instinct, attention to detail, judgment density — is where the closed labs still lead.But the market shift is obvious. Cheaper open-weight models do not need to beat frontier models outright. They only need to handle 80% of real work well enough. GLM‑5.2 may be the clearest sign yet that they can.The Fable 5 shutdown could not have been better timed for https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F.

Post 2

GLM‑5.2 can often do the job. The issue is that you may need three or four prompts to get what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 can often land in one.

Post 3

That gap is hard to see on benchmarks. Benchmarks measure whether a model can solve the task. Real work measures how much steering it needs before the answer becomes usable.

Post 4

Call it taste, instinct, attention to detail, or judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 is the ability to infer what matters before the user spells it out.

Post 5

Closed labs still have more of it. GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are often better at understanding the task earlier, pushing through ambiguity, catching small errors and finishing the work with less handholding.

Post 6

But the open-weight shift is real. GLM‑5.2 does not need to beat Fable 5. It only needs to be cheap, available and good enough for 80% of real tasks.

Post 7

Post 8

Post 9

9. The factual/citation scaffold to add

You can make the post far more defensible by adding a small evidence spine:

https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F describes GLM‑5.2 as a long-horizon flagship model with a 1M-token context window and an MIT open-source license, and its published table shows large jumps over GLM‑5.1 on coding benchmarks like Terminal Bench 2.1.Anthropic described Fable 5 as exceeding any model it had previously made generally available, especially on long and complex tasks, but marked Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access unavailable three days after launch.GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are both explicitly positioned by their labs for complex professional and agentic work, where less steering and better judgment matter.

Then your opinion lands harder because the facts are anchored.

10. Important correction: “open source” vs “open-weight”

Your draft says:

Open source models are missing a level of intelligence…

For GLM‑5.2, “open source” is defensible because the Hugging Face page says “MIT open-source license.”  But in AI discourse, open-weight is often more precise. A model can have open weights while still not being “open source” in the full software sense of training data, training code, data filters, post-training recipes and eval harnesses.

Better:

Open-weight models are missing a level of intelligence that benchmarks do not measure.

Or:

Open-weight/open-source models are catching up fast, but they still miss the invisible layer benchmarks do not measure.

Best:

Open-weight models are closing the capability gap before they close the judgment gap.

That line is excellent.

11. Important correction: “US government gave https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F this opening”

This is punchy but a little too monocausal. GLM‑5.2 did not succeed only because Fable 5 was suspended. It shipped with real improvements: 1M context, stronger coding benchmarks, open weights, MIT licensing, and easy drop-in usage in Claude Code-like workflows. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s own docs say GLM‑5.2 is live for GLM Coding Plan users and can be switched into Claude Code, including a 1M context suffix and effort mapping.

Better:

The Fable 5 shutdown did not create GLM‑5.2’s capability. But it created the perfect attention vacuum.

Or:

The U.S. government did not make GLM‑5.2 good. It made everyone look for an alternative at the exact moment GLM‑5.2 became good enough.

That is the best version.

12. Stronger “Fable 5 was overkill” argument

Original:

Fable 5 was overkill for 80% of vibe coding tasks anyway.

This is good, but you can make it more analytical:

Fable 5 was a Ferrari doing grocery runs for most vibe-coding sessions.

Or more serious:

Most vibe-coding tasks do not need the most capable model on Earth. They need fast iteration, cheap tokens, decent taste, long context, and enough autonomy to move through a codebase.

Best:

Fable 5 was not necessary for 80% of vibe coding. It was just nice to have because it collapsed the number of turns.

That connects back to the core thesis.

13. The “judgment density” section

This should be the intellectual centre of the post.

Write:

The missing capability is not just IQ. It is judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 shows up in tiny places:choosing the right abstraction without being told;
not overbuilding;
preserving the user’s taste;
knowing which edge case matters;
noticing when a spec is underdetermined;
asking one good question instead of generating three bad variants;
keeping the goal alive across edits;
finishing the last 10% without prompting.
Benchmarks rarely measure this because it is not one answer. It is how many interventions the user has to make before the work feels done.

That is a standout section.

14. The “turn tax” section

Use this:

The hidden cost of weaker models is not just tokens. It is turns.A cheap model that needs four prompts may still be cheaper in dollars, but it is not always cheaper in attention. The real unit is not cost per token. It is cost per completed decision.

This is excellent because it acknowledges GLM‑5.2’s value without pretending every task should use it.

Better still:

For many tasks, GLM‑5.2 wins on dollar cost and loses on human steering cost. The question is which cost matters more.

15. The routing framework you should add

Turn the post into practical advice:

Use GLM‑5.2 forUse GPT‑5.5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 forroutine vibe codingambiguous product decisionsscaffoldingtaste-sensitive frontendrefactors with clear instructionsunclear architecture choiceslong-context codebase searchhigh-stakes reasoningrepetitive implementationone-shot strategic synthesischeap parallel attemptsfinal polishcode migration drafts“figure out what I mean” tasksbulk generationtasks where steering is expensive

Suggested line:

GLM‑5.2 is becoming the default worker. Closed models remain the architect, editor and taste layer.

That is very strong.

16. The “model stack” idea

This is a genius-level practical solution:

Do not think of this as GLM versus Fable. Think of it as routing.Use a closed model to define the spec, taste, architecture and acceptance criteria. Use GLM‑5.2 to execute cheap bulk work. Use the closed model again to review, compress and polish.

This is the near-term production workflow.

Call it:

frontier sandwiching

Process:

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable writes the spec and acceptance criteria.

GLM‑5.2 executes the implementation.

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable reviews the result and catches judgment errors.

Suggested paragraph:

The winning workflow may not be choosing one model. It may be using frontier models for judgment and open models for labor. Let the closed model decide what good looks like. Let GLM‑5.2 do the cheap passes. Then bring the frontier model back for review.

That is more useful than a model ranking.

17. The “benchmarks are measuring solvedness, not independence” point

Most coding benchmarks measure whether a model eventually gets a correct answer. But users care about independence.

Use this:

Benchmarks often measure solvedness. Builders care about independence.Did it infer the missing requirement?
Did it avoid the dumb default?
Did it notice the visual mismatch?
Did it preserve the concept through revisions?
Did it stop at the right level of complexity?
Did it know when not to touch something?
Did it finish without being babysat?

That is a key distinction.

18. The “one prompt vs four prompts” benchmark idea

Propose a new benchmark:

Prompts-to-Production

Metric:

Give models the same messy user request. Measure how many user interventions are required before a human evaluator would ship the output.

Subscores:
first-pass usefulness
number of clarification turns
number of correction turns
number of taste fixes
number of bug fixes
number of regressions introduced
final acceptance time

user cognitive load

Suggested wording:

We need benchmarks that score not just final answer quality, but intervention count. A model that reaches 90% after one prompt is not equivalent to a model that reaches 90% after four.

That is exactly your argument.

19. Obscure thought input: “the last-mile cognition gap”

This is what GLM‑5.2 may still lack.

Open models are increasingly good at the first 80% and surprisingly good at the next 10%. The last 10% is where frontier labs still earn their money: taste, defaults, edge cases, cohesion, and knowing when the answer is finished.

Line:

The intelligence gap has moved from “can it do the task?” to “can it finish without making me manage the task?”

That is excellent.

20. Obscure thought input: “defaults are intelligence”

This is one of the best deeper ideas.
Open models often fail not because they cannot follow instructions, but because they choose weaker defaults when instructions are incomplete.
Use:
A lot of frontier-model intelligence lives in defaults. When the user underspecifies, what does the model assume? Does it choose the tasteful layout, the safer architecture, the cleaner abstraction, the narrower scope, the more useful answer? That is where closed models still feel ahead.
That is exactly the invisible quality.
21. Obscure thought input: “taste is compressed experience”
This is strong:
Taste is not vibes. Taste is compressed experience. It is knowing which detail will matter later.
Expanded:

When people say a model has better taste, they usually mean it has internalised more examples of what good work looks like and can apply that pattern before being explicitly instructed. That is why it saves prompts.

22. Obscure thought input: “cheap tokens do not equal cheap outcomes”

This belongs in the post.

Cheap tokens are not the same as cheap outcomes. If the model needs more supervision, the user becomes the missing compute.

That is a killer line.

Another:

When the model is cheaper but needs more steering, the human becomes the premium token.

Excellent.

23. Obscure thought input: “availability is capability”

The Fable 5 shutdown makes this point:

A slightly worse model that is available beats a better model behind a policy wall.

Suggested paragraph:
In AI, availability is now a capability. A model can be objectively better and still lose workflows if it cannot be accessed, routed, automated or trusted to stay online.
That directly supports the Fable/GLM angle.

24. Obscure thought input: “geopolitical routing”

The Fable 5 ban created a sovereignty/availability problem. The response is not just users switching models. It is organisations learning to route across jurisdictions.

Use:

The Fable 5 shutdown taught builders a brutal lesson: model quality is not enough. Jurisdiction, export control, uptime, pricing, and political risk are now part of the model selection stack.

This is very strong.

25. Obscure thought input: “the substitution trap”

Governments may think restricting frontier models slows capability diffusion. But if the next-best alternative is good enough and open-weight, restrictions can accelerate adoption of less controllable models.

Suggested:
The substitution trap is that banning the best closed model can push users toward open models that are less governable, more portable and harder to recall.
That is a major strategic insight.
26. Better “Unban Fable 5” phrasing
“Unban Fable 5” is punchy. Keep it as a final line if the audience is builder Twitter.
But for credibility, alternatives:
Restore Fable 5.

Bring Fable 5 back.

Do not force the market into substitutes.

Put Fable 5 back under transparent rules.

Reopen Fable 5 with a clear, appealable safety framework.

Best practical version:

Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.

Best viral version:

Unban Fable 5.
Use both:
Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.Unban Fable 5.
27. Missing caution: Fable access was already going to change
Anthropic’s launch page said Fable 5 would be included in Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans through June 22, then move to usage credits on June 23, capacity permitting.  So avoid implying the model was guaranteed to remain freely available in the same form. How I Built Safar With Figma Make, Figma Weavy, MCP, Supabase, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe, Canva, and GitHub

This document explains how I built Safar for the Figma hackathon.

It is written as a practical build story, not a technical code document. The goal is to show how I used Figma Make, Figma Weavy, clear product instructions, focused prompting, MCP-connected tools, Supabase, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe, Canva, GitHub, and continuous testing to move from idea to working product flow quickly.

I Started With a Clear Product Definition

Before building screens or connecting backend tools, I first defined what Safar needed to be.

Safar is a tourist e-visa eligibility checker and assisted application platform. It helps travelers check whether they can apply, understand which documents they need, upload those documents, pay transparently, and track application status in one place.

The early product rules kept the whole build focused:

Eligibility checking should work without login.
One account should manage multiple family members.
Every application should be reviewed by a real human before submission.
Fees should always be transparent: government fee, Safar service fee, and total.
Applicant, admin, and partner flows should stay separate.
Status should always use icon, color, and text, not color alone.
The product should feel calm, trustworthy, and simple because visa applications are high-stakes.

These rules became the foundation for the full app.

I Created the Guidelines First

The first major step was creating a guidelines.md document inside Figma Make.

I used it as the product and design rulebook for Safar. It included:

Product purpose
Brand colors
Typography
Layout rules
Card, button, input, progress bar, and status badge behavior
Mobile-first design rules
Navigation rules
Fee display rules
Applicant, admin, and partner role rules
Things that should never be changed

This helped Figma Make keep the design consistent across the app instead of creating random layouts for every screen.

The design direction was:

Deep green for trust
Warm gold as an accent
Warm off-white background
Inter font
Mobile-first layout around a 390px baseline
Clear cards, simple inputs, visible progress, and readable status badges

I did not treat the guidelines as a one-time file. I improved them through conversation first, then started asking Figma Make to build screens.

I Saved the Core Documents Before Building

Before starting the actual design and build, I saved the important planning documents in the project workspace so I could keep referring back to them.

These documents included:

Product guidelines
First Figma Make prompt
Build process notes
Security notes
Testing notes
Landing page copy
Video script
Data pipeline plan
Visual and video scene workflow notes

This helped me avoid losing context and made the workflow more structured. Whenever I needed to improve a screen or flow, I could refer back to the same product rules instead of explaining everything again from scratch.

I Used Supabase as the Backend Foundation

After the product flow and design direction were clear, I used Supabase as the backend foundation.

Supabase handled the core backend needs:

User authentication
Session restoration
Applicant, admin, and partner roles
Application records
Family member records
Document checklist storage
Private document file storage
Application status updates
Edge Functions for backend actions

The product needed separate flows for applicants, admins, and partners, so role-based access was important from the beginning.

Applicants could start or resume applications, upload documents, pay fees, track status, and view approved visa documents.

Admins could review applications, check uploaded documents, request changes, approve documents, upload visa outcomes, and update application status.

Partners had a limited dashboard where they could only see assigned applications and perform limited actions.

I Used Figma Make to Generate Supabase Table Prompts

One part that helped me move quickly was using Figma Make to prepare the Supabase database structure.

Instead of manually planning every table from scratch, I asked Figma Make to generate ready-to-use Supabase SQL prompts for the database tables.

Figma Make helped prepare the table structure for:

User profiles
Applications
Application members
Documents
Country requirements
Requirement reviews
Scrape logs
Roles and statuses

I then copied the generated SQL into Supabase and ran it there. The tables were created quickly, and I did not face schema bugs during that step.

This saved setup time and helped me move faster from idea to working product flow.

I Connected Supabase With MCP to Speed Up Backend Work

After the tables were ready, I connected Supabase through MCP-supported tooling so the AI-assisted workflow could help with backend implementation faster.

This made it easier to connect the frontend flow with backend actions.

Using Supabase MCP and connected tooling helped move faster on:

Authentication
Role-based routing
Application creation
Document upload flow
Payment flow connection
Application status updates
Edge Function setup
Admin and partner dashboard behavior

This was useful because I did not have to manually translate every product requirement into backend structure from scratch.

I Used Edge Functions for Server-Side Workflows

For backend workflows that should not run directly in the frontend, I used Supabase Edge Functions.

These supported important product actions such as:

Creating applications
Uploading documents
Starting payment checkout
Handling Stripe payment confirmation
Updating application status
Supporting admin actions
Connecting Firecrawl live data lookup

This helped keep sensitive work on the server side and kept the frontend cleaner.

I Built the Figma Make Prototype Section by Section

After the guidelines were ready, I started building the screens in Figma Make.

The homepage was built around a calm, trust-focused message. It included:

A clear hero section
Primary call-to-action
Animated nationality text concept
Destination country cards
Live fee display
Coming soon country chips
How-it-works section
Footer and bottom navigation

Then I moved into the eligibility flow:

Select nationality
Select destination
Select visa duration or travel details
Add traveler details
View eligibility result
Start application after login or sign-up

The key rule was that eligibility checking should not require login. That was repeated often because it was one of the most important product decisions.

I Created Consistent Visuals and Video Scenes With Figma Weavy

Alongside the product screens, I created consistent visual assets and video scenes for Safar. This helped make the hackathon submission feel more complete and visually connected.

I used Figma Weavy as part of the visual creation workflow. Inside that workflow, I used Google Imagen4 to create consistent and accurate images that matched the Safar product story and brand direction.

Before generating the visuals, I first created the character and scene direction in Claude. I used Claude to prepare:

Positive prompts for the characters
Negative prompts to avoid inconsistent or unwanted results
Character consistency notes
Scene-by-scene visual direction
Clear image style instructions

After that, I generated the character references and downloaded the strongest outputs. I then imported those references into Figma Weavy.

To keep the scenes consistent, I used Cedence Reference 2.0 through the reference loader. I attached the reference images with the prompts so the new scenes could follow the same character identity, style, and visual direction.

The process was:

Create character direction in Claude.
Write positive and negative prompts for consistency.
Generate strong reference images with Google Imagen4 inside Figma Weavy.
Download the best character references.
Import the references back into Figma Weavy.
Attach the references to scene prompts using Cedence Reference 2.0.
Convert the reference images into different scenes.
Combine the scenes in Canva.
Export the final visuals or video assets.
Upload the final assets to the website or submission materials.

This helped me avoid random visuals. Instead of generating every image from scratch, I reused reference-based prompting so the characters, mood, and visual story stayed consistent across scenes.

I Integrated Firecrawl for Live Visa Requirement Data

Firecrawl was added to support live visa requirement and fee lookup.

The goal was to avoid relying only on static visa information.

The flow was:

The frontend asks for eligibility or fee information.
The Supabase Edge Function checks cached data first.
If the data is missing or outdated, Firecrawl searches or scrapes official visa information sources.
The result is normalized into the format the app needs.
The data is cached for around 48 hours.
The UI can show whether the result came from live lookup or fallback data.

I also included an admin-facing live data toggle so Firecrawl usage could be paused or resumed to manage credits.

I Used AWS Rekognition for Identity Liveness Verification

To add a layer of identity confidence before the human review step, I integrated AWS Rekognition for face liveness detection.

The liveness check was triggered at the point of application submission to verify that a real person was submitting the application.

The flow was:

The applicant is prompted to complete a face liveness session before submission.
The frontend uses the AWS Amplify FaceLivenessDetector component to capture the session.
The session result is sent to a Supabase Edge Function for server-side verification.
AWS Rekognition returns a confidence score confirming whether the session was live.
If liveness is confirmed above the required threshold, the application moves forward.
If the check fails or the confidence is too low, the applicant is asked to retry.

This helped protect the platform from fraudulent or bot-submitted applications without adding significant friction to the genuine applicant experience.

I Used Stripe Sandbox for Payments

Stripe sandbox was used to build and test the payment flow safely before production.

The payment flow was designed around transparency:

User reviews the government fee.
User reviews the Safar service fee.
User sees the total.
User accepts the no-refund policy.
User is redirected to Stripe Checkout.
Stripe confirms payment.
The application status updates after successful payment.

Stripe Checkout was used instead of collecting card details directly in the app.

The Stripe webhook was connected through the backend so the application could still be marked as paid and submitted even if the browser redirect failed.

I Used GitHub as Part of the Build Environment

GitHub was connected as part of the broader build and deployment environment.

It helped keep the project organized and ready for versioning, deployment, and future collaboration.

The main development process was driven through Figma Make, Supabase, MCP tooling, and connected services, while GitHub supported the overall project workflow.

I Built the Applicant Dashboard Around the Real User Flow

The applicant dashboard was built around what users actually need after checking eligibility.

The dashboard supported:

Starting a new application
Resuming a draft application
Uploading required documents
Paying application fees
Tracking application status
Viewing payment status
Viewing approved visa documents when available

The application flow inside the dashboard was simplified into:

Trip setup
Documents
Payment
Application tracking

This kept the user journey easy to understand.

I Built the Document Flow Around Occupation-Based Requirements

The document checklist was generated based on the applicant's profile and occupation.

Base required documents included:

Passport
CNIC or national ID
Passport-size photograph
Bank statement
Return flight ticket
Hotel or accommodation proof

Occupation-specific documents included:

Employment letter for job holders
Salary slips for job holders
Business proof for business owners
Enrollment letter for students
NOC for government employees

This made the product more useful than a generic checklist because different applicants need different documents.

I Improved the Upload Flow After Testing

During testing, some document upload states needed improvement.

Instead of rebuilding the whole flow, I focused on the specific upload problem.

The improvements included:

Making sure loading states always clear after upload success or failure
Adding upload timeout behavior
Compressing large camera images before upload
Showing faster previews
Marking documents as uploaded immediately after success
Moving users to the next pending document faster

This made the document flow feel smoother and more reliable.

I Created Separate Admin and Partner Dashboards

The admin and partner dashboards were kept separate from the applicant flow.

Admin dashboard capabilities included:

View application queue
Review uploaded documents
Request document changes
Upload approved visa documents
Approve or update application status

Partner dashboard restrictions included:

Partners only see assigned applications.
Partners cannot access full admin review tools.
Partners cannot manage other partners.
Partners cannot access monitoring sections.
Partners can update status, request documents, and add notes.

This helped keep access clear and safer.

I Tested Before Making Changes

One important practice I followed was testing or checking the current state before making changes.

Before asking Figma Make or the AI assistant to update something, I first looked at what was already working and what was not.

For example, before changing a flow or screen, I checked:

What the user currently sees
Which step is working
Which part feels confusing
Whether the issue is visual, product-related, or technical
Whether the change could break another screen or flow

This helped avoid unnecessary changes. Instead of rebuilding a whole page, I could fix the exact problem.

The same approach was used after changes as well. I tested the main flows again to confirm the update actually worked.

I Did Not Try to Do Too Much in One Prompt

One of the biggest lessons was to avoid overloading a single prompt.

Instead of asking Figma Make to create too many flows, screens, states, and backend assumptions in one message, I broke the work into smaller parts.

The better approach was:

Build one screen or section at a time.
Give a clear problem statement.
Mention the exact user goal.
Mention what should be changed.
Mention what should not be changed.
Review the output before moving to the next part.

This made the AI output cleaner and easier to control.

For example, instead of asking for the whole application flow at once, I worked through the product in focused parts:

Homepage
Eligibility checker
Eligibility result
Sign-up flow
Applicant dashboard
Document checklist
Document upload
Payment summary
Admin dashboard
Partner dashboard

This kept the design and logic more stable.

I Used Clear Problem Statements

Whenever something needed improvement, I tried to explain the problem clearly instead of saying only “make it better.”

A useful prompt included:

What is wrong right now
Why it matters for the user
What outcome I want
Which part should stay the same

For example, if the fee section was too crowded, the prompt needed to explain that users may miss the total amount and that the hierarchy should be improved while keeping the three-line fee breakdown.

This made the AI behave more like a product teammate instead of randomly redesigning things.

I Used User Stories and Acceptance Criteria

For important flows, I used a user-story style.

Example:

As an applicant, I want to check my visa eligibility without creating an account, so I can understand my options before sharing personal details.

Acceptance criteria:

The user can start from the homepage.
The user can select passport, destination, and occupation.
The user can see the result without login.
The result shows required documents, fees, and processing time.
Login is only required when starting the application.

This helped the AI understand the product logic, not only the visual layout.

I Used Component Selection for Targeted Edits

When a screen needed improvement, I did not always rewrite the full prompt.

For small fixes, I edited directly.

For more complex fixes, I selected the exact component or section inside Figma Make and asked AI to improve only that part.

Examples:

Select a card and ask it to improve readability.
Select the fee section and ask it to improve hierarchy.
Select a form and ask it to make labels clearer.
Select a status badge and ask it to use icon, color, and text.

This reduced the chance of the AI changing unrelated parts of the design.

I Cleared the Chat After Every Few Prompts

Another practice that worked well was clearing the chat after every two or three prompts.

This helped keep the context clean and reduced prompt drift.

My workflow was:

Ask for a focused update.
Review the output.
Edit small things manually.
Ask for one targeted improvement if needed.
Clear the chat after the section felt stable.
Continue with the next screen or flow.

This made the AI follow the latest design patterns without carrying too much old context.

I Tested the Main Flows Before Finalizing

Testing was part of the process, not only something at the end.

The key flows I checked included:

Eligibility checker without login
Account creation
Single applicant application flow
Family application flow
Document upload
Document re-upload after rejection
Admin application review
Requirement change review
Liveness check behavior
Telegram update flow
Mobile browser experience
Stripe sandbox payment flow

Before changing important parts, I checked what was already working. After changing them, I tested again to make sure the fix did not break the journey.

What Made This Workflow Work

The process worked because I did not treat AI as a one-shot builder.

I treated it like a product team assistant.

The most useful practices were:

Start with clear product rules.
Create guidelines before asking for screens.
Test before changing things.
Do not put too much into one prompt.
Build one screen or section at a time.
Use clear problem statements.
Use user stories and acceptance criteria.
Select components for focused edits.
Edit small things manually.
Clear chat context after every few prompts.
Use Figma Weavy, Google Imagen4, reference images, and Canva for consistent visual assets.
Use MCP and connected tools for faster backend setup.
Use Supabase SQL prompts to quickly create the backend structure.
Use Firecrawl for live data instead of relying only on static content.
Use Stripe sandbox before production payments.
Keep testing the actual user flow.

Reusable Process for Future Builds

This same process can be reused for other products:

Define the product in one clear paragraph.

Lock the most important product rules.

Create a guidelines file before designing screens.

Save supporting documents in the workspace.

Build one screen or section at a time.

Use focused prompts with clear outcomes.

Test the current state before making changes.

Select components for targeted improvements.

Clear the chat after every few prompts.

Use AI to generate backend structure and setup prompts.

Copy reviewed setup prompts into tools like Supabase where needed.

Connect MCP tools to speed up implementation.

Use external services only where they solve a real product problem.

Test the end-to-end user journey before final submission.

Companion Documentation I Created for Reuse
Alongside this Safar-specific hackathon process, I also created a shorter reusable AI build playbook that can be shared with other founders, builders, or teams.

The companion document removes Safar-specific implementation details and turns the workflow into a repeatable process for other use cases, such as:

SaaS products
Landing pages
Mobile app prototypes
Admin dashboards
Document upload and OCR flows
Internal tools
Marketplace products
Hackathon builds

The purpose of the companion document is to show the process behind the build, not the private code or technical setup.

It explains how to start with a guidelines file, build in small prompts, test before changing, use component-level edits, and connect tools like Supabase MCP, GitHub, Firecrawl, Stripe, and backend functions only when the product flow needs them.

Support file you can reuse for any other project with best practices: https://t.co/v8WCpsq9V1

Final Summary

I built Safar by combining product thinking, Figma Make, focused prompting, Supabase, MCP-connected tools, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe sandbox, GitHub, Canva, Figma Weavy, and continuous testing.

The most important part was not asking AI to do everything at once.

I created clear guidelines first, built section by section, tested before changing, used focused prompts, and connected the right backend tools only when the product flow needed them.

This process helped me move quickly while still keeping the product structured, understandable, and ready to explain as part of the Figma hackathon submission.
